urceolate.why: Common in many Ericaceae flowers such as Arbutus and Vaccinium.

poricidal.plain: Releasing pollen through small pores instead of long slits.
poricidal.formal: Dehiscing through terminal or subterminal pores.

husk.plain: An outer covering around a nut or seed-bearing structure.
husk.formal: A fleshy, fibrous, or leathery outer fruit/perianth-derived layer surrounding a nut.
husk.where: Look around a walnut before the hard shell is exposed.
husk.why: A husked nut is a strong Juglandaceae fruit cue.

chambered-pith.plain: Stem pith divided into a series of little internal chambers.
chambered-pith.formal: Pith interrupted by transverse partitions or diaphragms.
chambered-pith.where: Visible in a clean twig cross/longitudinal section when appropriate.
chambered-pith.why: A useful secondary Juglans twig character.

annular-stipule-scar.plain: A ring-like scar left around the twig by a stipule.
annular-stipule-scar.formal: An encircling nodal scar produced by a sheathing stipule.
annular-stipule-scar.where: Inspect a sycamore twig at a node after leaf/stipule fall.

aliases: male and female flowers on one plant
monoecious.plain: One individual plant carries separate male and female flowers.
monoecious.formal: A sexual system in which staminate and pistillate flowers occur on the same individual.
monoecious.where: Compare flower types on the same plant.
monoecious.why: Useful in Platanus, Juglans, and many other wind-pollinated trees.

stipe.plain: The stalk of a fern frond below the leafy blade.
stipe.formal: The petiole-like basal stalk of a fern frond.
stipe.where: Follow the frond from the rhizome up to the first blade divisions.
stipe.why: Basic vocabulary for reading fern architecture.

pinna.plain: One primary division or leaflet-like section of a divided fern frond.
pinna.formal: A primary segment of a pinnate fern blade.
pinna.where: Look at the first major divisions along the rachis.
pinna.why: Helps describe fern division patterns consistently.

pinnule.plain: A smaller division of a pinna.
pinnule.formal: A secondary division of a pinnate fern frond.
pinnule.where: Look within a pinna for the next level of subdivision.

sorus.plain: A cluster of spore-producing structures on a fern.
sorus.formal: An aggregation of sporangia on a fern frond.
sorus.where: Usually on the underside or margin of a fertile frond.
sorus.why: Sorus position and shape are major fern-identification characters.

sporangium.plain: A tiny structure that produces spores.
sporangium.where: Look within a fern sorus under magnification.
sporangium.why: It is the actual spore-producing unit grouped into sori.

false-indusium.plain: A rolled-over fern leaf margin that covers the sori like a protective flap.
false-indusium.formal: A recurved or modified laminar margin sheltering marginal sori, rather than a separate true indusial membrane.
false-indusium.where: Inspect the edge of a fertile cliffbrake frond from below.
false-indusium.why: A signature teaching character for many local cheilanthoid Pteridaceae.

heterophylly.plain: One plant makes noticeably different leaf forms under different conditions.
heterophylly.formal: Production of morphologically distinct leaf types on the same individual, often in response to environment or developmental stage.
heterophylly.where: Compare submerged and emergent leaves on the same aquatic plant.
heterophylly.why: Aquatic plants can look like different species above and below water.

phyllode.plain: A flattened leaf-like structure that functions like a blade even when the usual blade is reduced.
phyllode.formal: A flattened photosynthetic petiole or modified leaf axis functioning in place of a conventional lamina.
phyllode.where: In the local Sagittaria lesson, inspect the narrow submerged leaf-like structures.
phyllode.why: It explains why submerged Sagittaria can look unlike the emergent plant.

enantiostyly.plain: Flowers occur in left- and right-handed forms because the style and stamens switch sides.
enantiostyly.formal: A floral polymorphism in which reproductive organs are reciprocally deflected to opposite sides in different flowers.
enantiostyly.why: It is a memorable reproductive morphology lesson and pollination adaptation.

salverform.plain: A flower with a long narrow tube that suddenly opens into a flat face.
salverform.formal: A sympetalous corolla with an elongated narrow tube and abruptly spreading limb.
salverform.where: View the flower from the side.
salverform.why: Corolla shape is a useful descriptive and comparative character.

staminate.plain: A flower that functions as male and bears stamens but no functional pistil.
staminate.formal: A unisexual flower bearing functional stamens and lacking a functional gynoecium.
staminate.where: Inspect the upper flower clusters of the Stillingia inflorescence.
staminate.why: Separates male from female flower roles in unisexual inflorescences.

pistillate.plain: A flower that functions as female and bears a pistil but no functional stamens.
pistillate.formal: A unisexual flower bearing a functional gynoecium and lacking functional stamens.
pistillate.where: Inspect the lower portion of the Stillingia inflorescence.
pistillate.why: Helps read the male-above/female-below organization of the local Stillingia anchor.

pollinarium.plain: The whole milkweed pollen-transfer unit, usually two pollinia linked by connecting arms to a small central clip.
pollinarium.formal: A pollen-transfer complex consisting of pollinia connected by translator arms to a corpusculum.
pollinarium.where: Look at the tiny removable pollen apparatus associated with the stigmatic slits of a milkweed gynostegium.
pollinarium.why: It explains how milkweed pollen is removed and transferred as a single mechanical unit rather than loose grains.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.focus: Look for the two pollen masses joined through the central transport apparatus.

corpusculum.plain: The tiny central clip-like part of a milkweed pollinarium that catches on a pollinator.
corpusculum.formal: The central hardened body of the pollinarium that connects translator arms leading to the pollinia.
corpusculum.where: Look at the center of a detached milkweed pollinarium between the two pollen masses.
corpusculum.why: It is the mechanical attachment point that helps a pollinator pull the pollinarium from the flower.

real_photo.label: Pollinarium showing the central corpusculum
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of a milkweed pollinarium
real_photo.focus: The corpusculum is the small central connector between the arms leading to the two pollinia.
